title: In re Administrative Subpoena for Messaging Metadata
text:
SYLLABUS

An administrative subpoena for encrypted messaging metadata held by a communications provider must satisfy the reasonableness standard, and the provider retains standing to move to quash on behalf of its subscribers.

I. Holding

We hold that an administrative subpoena seeking encrypted messaging metadata — the routing records, timestamps, and account identifiers a provider generates in the ordinary course of carrying a message — is not self-executing. The agency must show that the metadata sought is relevant to a legitimate investigation, that the demand is definite, and that compliance is not unreasonably burdensome. title: Wexler Holdings v. Ardent Mutual Insurance
text:
SYLLABUS

Inadvertent disclosure of a privileged document during discovery does not waive attorney-client privilege where the holder took reasonable steps to prevent disclosure and promptly moved to claw the document back.

I. Holding

We hold that attorney-client privilege survives an inadvertent production. The inquiry is not whether a privileged document escaped, but whether the holder's precautions were reasonable in light of the volume of the production and the time allowed for review, and whether the clawback demand followed promptly on discovery of the error. title: Pellas Salvage Co. v. United States
text:
SYLLABUS

Sovereign immunity bars a maritime salvage claim against a vessel owned and operated by the United States absent an express waiver, and the Suits in Admiralty Act supplies the exclusive remedy where it applies.

I. Holding

We hold that a salvor who rescues a government vessel may not proceed in rem against that vessel. Sovereign immunity is not waived by the government's entry into maritime commerce, and the Suits in Admiralty Act, where it reaches the claim, displaces every other avenue of relief. title: Harrowgate Press v. Superior Court
text:
SYLLABUS

The public right of access to judicial records is presumptive, and a party seeking to seal a filing bears the burden of showing a compelling interest that outweighs the presumption and that no narrower remedy suffices.

I. Holding

We hold that sealing a filing requires findings on the record. A court may not seal a document wholesale where redaction would protect the interest asserted, and the party seeking secrecy — not the press, and not the public — carries the burden throughout.
